L52@P1: recursive proof composition); and (2) the prover’s work at each step is dominated
L53@P1: by two multiexponentiations of size O(|F|), providing the fastest prover in the literature, both asymptotically and concretely. Section 1.4 provides a detailed comparison between our approach and prior work.
L54@P1: 1.1 Folding Schemes
L55@P1: A folding scheme is defined with respect to an NP relation, and it is a protocol between an untrusted prover and a verifier. Both entities hold two N-sized
L56@P1: NP instances, and the prover in addition holds purported witnesses for both
L57@P1: instances. The protocol enables the prover and the verifier to output a single
L58@P1: N-sized NP instance, which we refer to as a folded instance. Furthermore, the
L59@P1: prover privately outputs a purported witness to the folded instance using purported witnesses for the original instances. Informally, a folding scheme guarantees
L60@P1: that the folded instance is satisfiable only if the original instances are satisfiable.
L61@P1: A folding scheme is said to be non-trivial if the verifier’s costs and the communication are lower in the case where the verifier participates in the folding scheme and
L62@P1: then verifies a purported NP witness for the folded instance than the case where
L63@P1: the verifier verifies purported NP witnesses for each of the original instances.
L64@P1: Several existing techniques exhibit the two-to-one reduction pattern of folding
L65@P1: schemes. Examples include the sumcheck protocol [35] and the split-and-fold
L66@P1: techniques in inner product arguments [11]. [30, App. A] provides further details.
L67@P1: Remark 1 (Folding Schemes vs. SNARKs). SNARKs for NP [7,23,24,29,36]
L68@P1: trivially imply a folding scheme for NP: given two NP instances u1 and u2 and
L69@P1: the corresponding witnesses, the prover proves u1 by producing a SNARK. The
L70@P1-2: verifier checks that SNARK and then sets u2 to be the folded instance. However,Nova: Recursive Zero-Knowledge Arguments from Folding Schemes 361
L71@P2: we construct a folding scheme for NP without relying on SNARKs (or more generally arguments of knowledge). Specifically, our folding scheme is weaker than
L72@P2: any argument of knowledge (succinct or otherwise) because it merely reduces the
L73@P2: satisfiability of two NP instances to the satisfiability of a single NP instance.1
L74@P2: To design a folding scheme for NP, we start with a popular NP-complete language that generalizes arithmetic circuit satisfiability: R1CS (Definition 10). As
L75@P2: we illustrate later, it is difficult to devise a folding scheme for R1CS. To address
L76@P2: this, we introduce a variant of R1CS, called relaxed R1CS, which, like R1CS,
L77@P2: not only characterizes NP, but, unlike R1CS, can support a folding scheme. The
L78@P2: following theorem captures the cryptographic and efficiency characteristics of
L79@P2: our folding scheme for relaxed R1CS.
L80@P2: Theorem 1. There exists a constant-round, public-coin, zero-knowledge folding
L81@P2: scheme for relaxed R1CS where for N-sized relaxed R1CS instances over a finite
L82@P2: field F with the same “structure” (i.e., R1CS coefficient matrices), the prover’s
L83@P2: work is Oλ(N), and the verifier’s work and the communication are both Oλ(1),
L84@P2: assuming the existence of any additively-homomorphic commitment scheme that
L85@P2: provides Oλ(1)-sized commitments to N-sized vectors over F (e.g., Pedersen’s
L86@P2: commitments), where λ is the security parameter.
L87@P2: Because our folding scheme is public coin, it can be made non-interactive in
L88@P2: the random oracle model using the Fiat-Shamir transform [22], and be instantiated (heuristically) in the standard model using a concrete hash function. We
L89@P2: rely on such a non-interactive folding scheme to construct IVC.
L90@P2: 1.2 IVC from Non-interactive Folding Schemes
L91@P2: We show how to realize IVC using a non-interactive version of our folding scheme
L92@P2: for relaxed R1CS. We refer to our construction as Nova.
L93@P2: Recall that an IVC is an argument of knowledge [29,36]
L94@P2: 2 for incremental

L98@P2: incremental step, the IVC prover produces a proof that the step was computed
L99@P2: correctly and it has verified a proof for the prior step. In other words, at each
L100@P2: incremental step, the IVC prover produces a proof of satisfiability for an augmented circuit that augments the circuit for F with a “verifier circuit” that
L101@P2: verifies the proof of the prior step. Recursively, the final proof proves the correctness of the entire incremental computation. A key aspect of IVC is that
L102@P2: neither the IVC verifier’s work nor the IVC proof size depends on the number of
L103@P2: 1 This work realizes IVC using our folding scheme. As IVC implies SNARKs (e.g.,
L104@P2: see [6]), one might wonder whether folding schemes are in general weaker than
L105@P2: SNARKs. However, existing constructions of IVC (including our own) rely on additional assumptions (§4.2), which the resulting IVC-based SNARK inherits. 2 An argument of knowledge for circuit satisfiability enables an untrusted polynomialtime prover to prove to a verifier the knowledge of a witness w such that C(w, x)= y,
L106@P2-3: where C is a circuit, x is some public input, and y is some public output.362 A. Kothapalli et al.
L107@P3: steps in the incremental computation. In particular, the IVC verifier only verifies
L108@P3: the proof produced at the last step of the incremental computation.
L109@P3: In Nova, we consider incremental computations, where each step of the incremental computation is expressed with R1CS (all the steps in the incremental
L110@P3: computation share the same R1CS coefficient matrices). At step i of the incremental computation, as in other approaches to IVC, Nova’s prover proves that
L111@P3: the step i was computed correctly. Furthermore, at step i, instead of verifying a
L112@P3: proof for step i−1 (as in traditional approaches to IVC), Nova’s approach treats
L113@P3: the computation at step i−1 as an R1CS instance and folds that into a running
L114@P3: relaxed R1CS instance. Specifically, at each step, Nova’s prover proves that it has
L115@P3: performed the step’s computation and has folded its prior step represented as an
L116@P3: R1CS instance into a running relaxed R1CS instance. In other words, the circuit
L117@P3: satisfiability instance that the prover proves at each incremental step computes
L118@P3: a step of the incremental computation and includes a circuit for the computation
L119@P3: of the verifier in the non-interactive folding scheme for relaxed R1CS.
L120@P3: A distinctive aspect of Nova’s approach to IVC is that it achieves the smallest
L121@P3: “verifier circuit” in the literature. Since the verifier’s costs in the non-interactive
L122@P3: version of the folding scheme for relaxed R1CS is Oλ(1), the size of the computation that Nova’s prover proves at each incremental step is ≈|F|, assuming Nsized vectors are committed with an Oλ(1)-sized commitments (e.g., Pedersen’s
L123@P3: commitments). In particular, the verifier circuit in Nova is constant-sized and
L124@P3: its size is dominated by two group scalar multiplications. Furthermore, Nova’s
L125@P3: prover’s work at each step is dominated by two multiexponentiations of size ≈|F|.
L126@P3: Note that Nova’s prover does not perform any FFTs, so it can be instantiated
L127@P3: efficiently using any cycles of elliptic curves where DLOG is hard.
L128@P3: With the description thus far, the size of an IVC proof (which is a purported
L129@P3: witness for the running relaxed R1CS instance) is Oλ(|F|). Instead of sending
L130@P3: such a proof to a verifier, at any point in the incremental computation, Nova’s
L131@P3: prover can prove the knowledge of a satisfying witness to the running relaxed
L132@P3: R1CS instance in zero-knowledge with an Oλ(log |F|)-sized succinct proof using
L133@P3: a zkSNARK that we design by adapting Spartan [38]. The following theorem
L134@P3: summarizes our key result.
L135@P3: Theorem 2. For any incremental function where each step of the incremental
L136@P3: function applies a (non-deterministic) function F, there exists an IVC scheme
L137@P3: with the following efficiency characteristics, assuming N-sized vectors are committed with an Oλ(1)-sized commitments.
L138@P3: – IVC proof sizes are O(|F|) and the verifier’s work to verify them is Oλ(|F|).
L139@P3: The prover’s work at each incremental step is ≈|F|. Specifically, the prover’s
L140@P3: work at each step is dominated by two multiexponentiations of size ≈|F|.
L141@P3: – Succinct zero-knowledge proofs of valid IVC proofs are size Oλ(log |F|), and
L142@P3: the verifier’s work to verify them is either Oλ(log |F|) or Oλ(|F|) depending
L143@P3: on the commitment scheme for vectors. The prover’s work to produce this
L144@P3-4: succinct zero-knowledge proof is Oλ(|F|).Nova: Recursive Zero-Knowledge Arguments from Folding Schemes 363
L145@P4: 1.3 Implementation and Performance Evaluation
L146@P4: We implement Nova as a library in about 6,000 lines of Rust [3]. The library is
L147@P4: generic over a cycle of elliptic curves and a hash function (used internally as the
L148@P4: random oracle). The library provides candidate implementations with the Pasta
L149@P4: cycle of elliptic curves [4] and Poseidon [2,26]. Finally, the library accepts F (i.e.,
L150@P4: a step of the incremental computation) as a bellperson gadget [1].
L151@P4: Recursion Overheads. We measure the size of Nova’s verifier circuit, as it determines the recursion overhead: the number of additional constraints that the prover
L152@P4: must prove at each incremental step besides proving an invocation of F.
L153@P4: We find that Nova’s verifier circuit is ≈20,000 R1CS constraints. This is the
L154@P4: smallest verifier circuit in the literature and hence Nova incurs the lowest recursion
L155@P4: overhead. Specifically, Nova’s recursion overhead is >10× lower than in SNARKbased IVC [6] with state-of-the-art per-circuit trusted setup SNARK [27], and over
L156@P4: 100× smaller than with a SNARK without trusted setup [21]. Compared to recent
L157@P4: works, Nova’s recursion overhead is over 7× lower than Halo’s [12], and over 2×
L158@P4: lower than the scheme of Bunz et al. [15] (Fig. 1).

L169@P4: Performance of Nova. We experiment with Nova on an Azure Standard
L170@P4: F32s v2 VM (16 physical CPUs, 2.70 GHz Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8168,
L171@P4: and 64 GB memory). In our experiments, we vary the number of constraints in
L172@P4: F. Our performance metrics are: the prover time, the verifier time, and proof
L173@P4: sizes. We measure these for Nova’s IVC scheme as well as its Spartan-based
L174@P4: zkSNARK to compress IVC proofs. Figure 2 depicts our results, and we find the
L175@P4: following.
L176@P4: – The prover’s per-step cost to produce an IVC proof and compress it scale
L177@P4: sub-linearly with the size of F (since the cost is dominated by two multiexponentiations, which scale sub-linearly due to the Pippenger algorithm and
L178@P4: parallelize better at larger sizes). When |F|≈ 220 constraints, the prover’s
L179@P4: per-step cost to produce an IVC proof is ≈1µs/constraint. For the same F,
L180@P4: the cost to produce a compressed IVC proof is ≈24µs/constraint.3

L183@P4-5: IVC proof every ≈240 steps, the overhead drops to ≈20%.364 A. Kothapalli et al.

L210@P5: 1.4 A More Detailed Comparison with Prior Work
L211@P5: Figure 3 compares Nova with prior approaches. Nova’s approach can be viewed
L212@P5: as taking Halo’s approach to the extreme. Specifically:
L213@P5: – At each incremental step, Halo’s verifier circuit verifies a “partial” SNARK.
L214@P5: This still requires Halo’s prover to perform |F|-sized FFTs and O(|F|) exponentiations (i.e., not an |F|-sized multiexponentiation). Whereas, in Nova,
L215@P5: the verifier circuit folds an entire NP instance representing computation at
L216@P5: the prior step into a running relaxed R1CS instance. This only requires Nova’s
L217@P5: prover to commit to a satisfying assignment of an ≈|F|-sized circuit (which
L218@P5: computes F and performs the verifier’s computation in a folding scheme for
L219@P5: relaxed R1CS), so at each step, Nova’s prover only computes an O(|F|)-
L220@P5: sized multiexponentiation and does not compute any FFTs. So, Nova’s prover
L221@P5: incurs lower costs than Halo’s prover, both asymptotically and concretely.
L222@P5: – The verifier circuit in Halo is of size Oλ(log |F|) whereas in Nova, it is Oλ(1).
L223@P5: Concretely, the dominant operations in Halo’s circuit is O(log |F|) group
L224@P5: scalar multiplications, whereas in Nova, it is two group scalar multiplications.
L225@P5: – Halo and Nova have the same proof sizes Oλ(log |F|) and verifier time Oλ(|F|).
L226@P5: B¨unz et al. [16] apply Halo’s approach to other polynomial commitment
L227@P5: schemes. Halo Infinite [10] generalizes the approach in Halo [12] to any homomorphic polynomial commitment scheme; they also obtain PCD (and hence IVC)
L228@P5: even when polynomial commitment schemes do not satisfy succinctness.
L229@P5: B¨unz et al. [15] propose a variant of the approach in Halo, where they realize
L230@P5: PCD (and hence IVC) without relying on succinct arguments. Specifically, they
L231@P5: first devise a non-interactive argument of knowledge (NARK) for R1CS with
L232@P5: Oλ(N)-sized proofs and Oλ(N) verification times for N-sized R1CS instances.
L233@P5: Then, they show that most of the NARK’s verifier’s computation can be deferred
L234@P5-6: by performing Oλ(1) work in the verifier circuit. For zero-knowledge, Nova reliesNova: Recursive Zero-Knowledge Arguments from Folding Schemes 365

L269@P6: and efficiency advantages over the work of B¨unz et al. [15]:

L277@P6: verifier circuit are both higher than in Nova by ≈4×.
L278@P6: – Proof sizes are Oλ(|F|) in their work, whereas in Nova, they are Oλ(log |F|).

L280@P6: argument, but unlike Nova, they do not specify how to do so in a concretely
L281@P6: efficient manner. Furthermore, using succinct arguments is inconsistent with

L288@P7: 1.5 An Overview of the Rest of the Paper
L289@P7: Section 2 provides the necessary background. Section 3 formally defines folding
L290@P7: schemes and their properties. In Sect. 4, we introduce a variant of R1CS called
L291@P7: relaxed R1CS for which we provide a folding scheme satisfying Theorem 1. Then,
L292@P7: in Sect. 5, we use a non-interactive version of the folding scheme (§4.2) to construct an IVC scheme and a scheme to compress IVC proofs satisfying Theorem 2
L293@P7: by assuming the existence of a zkSNARK for relaxed R1CS with logarithmicsized proofs. Finally, in Sect. 6, we construct such a zkSNARK.
L294@P7: 2 Preliminaries
L295@P7: Let F denote a finite field with |F| =2Θ(λ), where λ is the security parameter. Let ∼= denote computational indistinguishability with respect to a PPT adversary.
L296@P7: We globally assume that generator algorithms that produce public parameters
L297@P7: are additionally provided appropriate size bounds.
L298@P7: 2.1 A Commitment Scheme for Vectors over F
L299@P7: We require a commitment scheme for vectors over F that is additively homomorphic and succinct. We formally define these two properties and others noted
L300@P7: below in [30, App. F]. Below, we define the syntax for commitment schemes.
L301@P7: Definition 1 (A Commitment Scheme for Vectors). A commitment
L302@P7: scheme for Fm is a tuple of three protocols with the following interface.
L303@P7: – Gen(1λ,m) → pp: takes length parameter m; produces public parameters pp.
L304@P7: – Com(pp, v, r) → C: takes vector v ∈ Fm and r ∈ F; produces commitment C.
L305@P7: – Open(pp, C, v, r) →{0, 1}: verifies the opening of commitment C to v ∈ Fm.
L306@P7: A commitment scheme satisfies hiding (the commitment reveals no information),
L307@P7: binding (a PPT adversary cannot open a commitment to two different values),
L308@P7: and succinctness (the commitment size is logarithmic in the opening size).
L309@P7: 2.2 Non-interactive Arguments of Knowledge
L310@P7: Definition 2 (Non-Interactive Argument of Knowledge). Consider a
L311@P7: relation R over public parameters, structure, instance, and witness tuples. A noninteractive argument of knowledge for R consists of PPT algorithms (G,P, V)
L312@P7: and deterministic K, denoting the generator, the prover, the verifier and the
L313@P7-8: encoder respectively with the following interface.Nova: Recursive Zero-Knowledge Arguments from Folding Schemes 367
